title: Sovereign citizen gobbledygook never wins
summary: Australian law-firm article: pseudolaw never wins in court, worsens outcomes, is spread by paid gurus and is a growing security concern.

assertions.quote: SOVEREIGN CITIZEN ARGUMENTS DON'T WIN IN COURT AND MIGHT LAND YOU IN JAIL.
Pseudolaw does not work. It makes things worse for those who try it,
self-proclaimed gurus who are cashing in from people who pay to hear and follow their anti-government tirades
grew in Australia during the Covid-19 epidemic lockdowns
The movement originated in the United States with racist and religious beliefs
The Australian Federal Police have warned these groups have a potential for violence, fixation and harassment.
Threats against the judiciary in Victoria increased fourfold between 2023 and 2025.

verdicts.note: Judicial bodies in the US and Australia report threats and harassment from sovereign-citizen litigants, though not all threats come from them.
Examples include threats against law enforcement by a Freeman guru and an attempt to arrest a provincial judge; Freemen made up 4 of 86 offenders in a study of harassers of justice officials.
The FBI is quoted saying members threaten judges, law enforcement and government personnel.
FBI describes tactics to harass and intimidate law enforcement, court and government officials, including judges and prosecutors protected by the Court Security Improvement Act.
Review reports public administration and court employees are often targets of coercion and extortion in response to official documents.

assertions.quote: found these claimed court successes did not exist

verdicts.note: The one concrete win a guru cited was 'to be generous, dubious' (an unrelated foreign acquittal), and Clifford's claim that Freeman wins are hidden is unsupported; two examples, not a survey.
Promised successes are 'at best, rumour' and failures go undisclosed; one guru misdescribed his acquittal, but a few real wins on ordinary grounds exist.
